title: Combining information from texts
keyIdea: When two texts cover the same topic, sort what you find: facts in both texts (even in different words), facts only in Text A, and facts only in Text B. Some questions need both texts, because each holds part of the answer. If the texts disagree, check a third source before you write. A combined summary says each fact once, joins facts that go together, and adds no opinions or outside facts. Linking words show the link: both texts say, Text B adds, however.
familyTip: Read two short pieces on one topic, such as a leaflet and a web page about a local animal. Ask: what did both say? What did only one say? Did they disagree anywhere? Then say one summary sentence that uses both, such as 'Both say it is nocturnal, and the web page adds that it eats slugs.'

visual.caption: Text A: “Hedgehogs come out at night and eat worms.” Text B: “Hedgehogs are nocturnal and eat slugs.” Drag each fact, or tap it and then a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: sort hedgehog facts into Only A, Both or Only B, find which text answers a question, settle a clash, build one summary, join with linking words.

kid: Two texts on the same topic often share some facts. Each one also has facts the other does not. Sort them into three groups: in both texts, only in Text A, and only in Text B.
Watch for the same fact in different words. One text says hedgehogs come out at night. The other says they are nocturnal. That is one fact, so it goes in both.

Some questions need both texts. Text A says hedgehogs eat beetles and worms. Text B says they eat slugs. To answer 'What do they eat?', you need both. If the texts disagree, such as 5,000 or 7,000 spines, check a third source.
Now write one summary. Say each fact once and join facts that belong together. Leave out opinions and facts neither text gives. Linking words help: both texts say, Text B adds, however.
adult: Ages 9 to 10. This is US Common Core RI.4.9: integrate information from two texts on the same topic in order to write or speak about the subject knowledgeably. In England it sits under the Year 3–6 reading objective of retrieving and recording information from non-fiction, and the Year 5–6 writing objective of précising longer passages.

The skill has three parts. Comparison: what is shared, what is unique, and what clashes. Synthesis: one account that keeps each fact once and merges partial answers. Checking: a contradiction is settled with a third, trusted source, not by choosing the first or the more familiar text.

The lab uses two short hedgehog texts with facts checked against the People's Trust for Endangered Species and the British Hedgehog Preservation Society. Learners sort seven facts into a Venn diagram, match five questions to the text that answers them, settle 5,000 versus 7,000 spines with a third source (5,000 to 7,000), build a five-sentence summary, and join pairs with linking words.

Common mistakes. Children treat a fact in different words as two facts, or copy one text and ignore the other. Others repeat a fact in the summary, add opinions or facts from outside the texts, or settle a clash by picking the first text or averaging the numbers. Ask: where does each sentence of the summary come from?

practice.prompt: Text A: “Bats sleep in the day.” Text B: “Bats are active at night.” How do these relate?
choices: They say the same thing in different words
Text B adds a new topic
practice.hint: Does sleeping in the day mean being awake at night?
practice.explain: Sleeping in the day and being active at night describe the same habit, so the fact belongs in 'both texts'.

practice.prompt: Text A has {a} facts and Text B has {b} facts. {s} facts are in both. How many different facts are there in all?
practice.hint: Add the two lists, then take away the shared facts so you do not count them twice.
practice.explain: {a} + {b} counts each shared fact twice, so take {s} away: {a} + {b} − {s} = {=a+b-s} different facts.

practice.prompt: Text A says a tree is 30 m tall. Text B says 35 m. What should you do?
choices: Use 30 m because you read it first
practice.hint: Can you tell which is right from these two texts alone?
practice.explain: The texts disagree, so check a third, trusted source before you write a number.

practice.prompt: Text A has {a} facts. {s} of them are also in Text B. How many facts are only in Text A?
practice.hint: Take the shared facts away from Text A's facts.
practice.explain: Of Text A's {a} facts, {s} are shared, so {a} − {s} = {=a-s} are only in Text A.

practice.prompt: Which sentence combines two texts well?
choices: Both texts say foxes hunt at night, and Text B adds that they eat berries.
Foxes hunt at night. Foxes hunt at night.
practice.hint: Which sentence says each fact once and stays with the texts?
practice.explain: It keeps the shared fact once and adds Text B's new detail. The others repeat or give an opinion.

pool.prompt: Text A lists beetles and worms. Text B lists slugs. What is the full answer to 'What do hedgehogs eat?'
pool.hint: Does either text alone hold the whole list?
pool.explain: Each text holds part of the list, so combine them: beetles, worms and slugs.

pool.prompt: Which question needs both texts? Text A: what owls eat. Text B: where owls nest.
choices: What do owls eat, and where do they nest?
pool.hint: Which question asks for something from each text?
pool.explain: Food comes from Text A and nests from Text B, so that question needs both.

pool.prompt: A summary says 'Hedgehogs can fly.' Neither text says this. What is the slip?
choices: It adds a fact from neither text
pool.hint: Where did this sentence come from?
pool.explain: A combined summary only uses information from the texts. This sentence comes from neither.

pool.prompt: Text A: 5,000 spines. Text B: 7,000. A third source says 5,000 to 7,000. Which sentence is best?
choices: An adult has about 5,000 to 7,000 spines.
pool.hint: What does the checked source support?
pool.explain: The third source gives a range that includes both texts, so write the range. No source says 6,000.

pool.prompt: Which linking words fit? Text A: 'Moles dig tunnels.' Text B: 'Moles dig tunnels to catch worms.'
pool.hint: Does B disagree, or does it give more?
pool.explain: B agrees and gives a new detail (to catch worms), so 'Text B adds'.

pool.prompt: Which linking words fit? Text A: 'The pond froze in January.' Text B: 'The pond did not freeze this winter.'
pool.hint: Can the pond both freeze and not freeze in the same winter?
pool.explain: The texts contradict each other, so use 'However' and then check a third source.

pool.prompt: A Venn diagram has {x} facts in 'Only A', {y} in 'Both' and {z} in 'Only B'. How many facts does Text B give?
pool.hint: Text B's facts are the ones in its own part and in the middle.
pool.explain: Text B gives the shared facts and its own: {y} + {z} = {=y+z}.

pool.prompt: Two texts share {s} facts. A pupil's summary writes each shared fact twice. How many sentences should the pupil delete?
pool.hint: Each shared fact should appear once. How many extra copies are there?
pool.explain: Each of the {s} shared facts has one extra copy, so delete {s} sentences.

pool.prompt: Text A: 'Seals are mammals.' Text B: 'Seals breathe air and feed milk to their pups.' What does B do?
choices: It adds details that fit A
It repeats A word for word
pool.hint: Breathing air and feeding milk: do they fit with being a mammal?
pool.explain: Mammals breathe air and feed their young milk, so B adds supporting details.

pool.prompt: A pupil copies Text A and ignores Text B. What is the slip?
choices: The summary leaves out B's facts
pool.hint: Is the summary built from both texts?
pool.explain: Combining means using both texts. Copying one leaves out everything only B gives.
